rows.verified: Natural-rubber latex proteins can cause occupational asthma, dermatitis and urticaria.
Severe latex reactions are uncommon but can include anaphylaxis.
Powdered latex gloves can disperse latex proteins into the air when gloves are put on or removed.
Low-protein, powder-free single-use latex gloves reduce inhalation and skin exposure compared with powdered products.
Employers should first decide whether gloves are required and consider control methods that avoid exposure before relying on gloves.
Where gloves are needed, suitability should account for the hazard, contact duration, wearer, fit, dexterity and work environment.
Workers with an existing latex allergy should use latex-avoidance measures and may need gloves made from an alternative material.
Risk assessment should consider whether health surveillance for occupational asthma or dermatitis is needed where latex gloves are used.
Latex risk depends on protein content, powder, frequency of use, exposure route, sensitisation, task and individual susceptibility.
Latex evidence is product-, exposure-, worker- and sensitisation-specific and is not an exact parcel-level allergy probability.
Every workplace must have suitable and sufficient lighting for people to work and move safely.
Roads, manoeuvring areas, yards, pedestrian routes and other traffic areas need adequate lighting.
Lighting equipment should be maintained in good working order and covers should be kept clean.
Junctions, buildings, plant, pedestrian areas and regular vehicle-movement zones require particular attention.
Light positioning should account for tall vehicles or structures that can block illumination and create shadowed areas.
Lights should be positioned and angled to avoid dazzling drivers directly or through mirrors.
Work around moving vehicles during darkness should be adequately illuminated, including loading and unloading areas.
Emergency routes need sufficient lighting, with emergency lighting where failure of the primary system would create risk.
Lighting effectiveness depends on layout, shadows, glare, weather, vehicle height, maintenance, visual task and transitions between light levels.
Lighting evidence is route-, task-, layout-, visibility- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision or fall probability.
